+Design document for `challenged`, a job worker service written in Rust
+==============================================================
+
+The goal of this project is to write a job worker server with an API that allows clients to start and stop "jobs" - i.e. processes - on the server's machine, and to query their status and their output.
+
+The program will be composed of a library, containing the bulk of the code pertaining to job handling, the server-side gRPC API (including authentication), and the authorization scheme, and a small program that simply initializes and runs the server.
+
+In addition, a simple CLI binary (`challenger`) to use the API will also be included.
+
+Authentication
+--------------
+Authentication in the gRPC layer will be handled through mTLS; we'll use tonic's [rustls](https://github.com/rustls/rustls) support, which only supports strong authentication, key exchange and encryption (TLSv1.2 or 1.3 with ephemeral kex and AEAD ciphers).
+
+Tonic exposes a simple way to specify which CAs are trusted with regards to client certificates, so for authentication we'll require that a client's certificate is signed by a (hardcoded, for simplicity) dedicated CA and that it's not expired; the authenticated identity is then taken to be the common name stored in the certificate. We won't handle certificate revocation, but it could be handled by distributing a CRL or by checking OCSP status in the presence of a dedicated PKI.
+
+The client will also have to authenticate the server; we'll hardcode the server's certificate in the client as well. The client certificate will be specified at runtime, to allow for multiple identities to be demonstrated.
+
+Authorization scheme
+--------------------
+All authenticated users can start jobs - each job has an owner - and all authenticated users can query the status of a job. The users in a hardcoded list (`admin` and `root`) can stop and read the output of every job, while authenticated users can stop and read the output of their own jobs.
+
+API
+---
+The gRPC API is composed of a single `JobControl` service with five methods (`Start`, `Stop`, `GetInfo`, `GetOutput` and `StreamOutput`), detailed in [proto/jobcontrol.proto](proto/jobcontrol.proto). For simplicity, the API doesn't allow every cgroup parameter to be changed - for instance, the IO controller only allows `io.weight`.
+

pull_request.title: Lockless data structure to store job outputs
pull_request.body:
This changes the storage for the `JobOutput` messages that describe
the output of a job from an `RwLock<Vec<_>>` to a lockless,
append-only unrolled linked list that allows multiple readers and
one writer. As there doesn't seem to be something that quite fits
the purpose on crates.io, this is a new implementation.

Whether or not the performance of allocating and following nodes in
an unrolled linked list beats the occasional reallocations of a
`RwLock`ed vector remains to be seen, so it is not something that
should be used without a measurable reason and without extensive
vetting (it makes liberal use of `unsafe`, as one might imagine).

For the sake of this exercise, `concurrent-list` is stored as part
of the workspace of `challenged`, even though it is a completely
separate library and should be kept standalone. Right now it requires
the beta toolchain, because it uses the `unsafe_cell_raw_get` feature,
which will get stabilized in Rust 1.56.

We won't handle certificate revocation, but it could be handled by distributing a CRL or by checking OCSP status in the presence of a dedicated PKI.
+
+The client will also have to authenticate the server; we'll hardcode the server's certificate in the client as well. The client certificate will be specified at runtime, to allow for multiple identities to be demonstrated.
+
+Authorization scheme
+--------------------
+All authenticated users can start jobs - each job has an owner - and all authenticated users can query the status of a job. The users in a hardcoded list (`admin` and `root`) can stop and read the output of every job, while authenticated users can stop and read the output of their own jobs.
+
+API
+---
+The gRPC API is composed of a single `JobControl` service with five methods (`Start`, `Stop`, `GetInfo`, `GetOutput` and `StreamOutput`), detailed in [proto/jobcontrol.proto](proto/jobcontrol.proto). For simplicity, the API doesn't allow every cgroup parameter to be changed - for instance, the IO controller only allows `io.weight`.
+
+Design approach
+---------------
+A "job" consists of a program, with (optionally) some arguments, launched - if possible - in its own cgroup, with optional resource limits as decided by the client; we'll spawn the program with `/dev/null` as standard input, and a single pipe as standard output and error.
+
+We'll consider the job to be finished when our child process terminates; we then either kill the whole cgroup or ignore other processes (if cgroups are not available). Supporting daemonizing processes or cgroup-aware processes that create sub-cgroups is out of scope for this project.
+
+The output pipe could be closed before the process terminates - we'll maintain the illusion that further output is still possible, so that `StreamOutput` only terminates with the process itself. When the child dies, we drain and then close our end of the pipe - it could be that the child end of the pipe was smuggled to some other process, so we can't just assume that killing the cgroup will close it.
+
+The output chunks will be added to the in-memory log and sent through a broadcast channel so that `StreamOutput` can acquire some lock, read the past output (depending on the data structure that we'll end up using, this could end up being quite cheap) and then start listening to the channel to receive the new output as it comes (an alternative would be to write the output to a file, and have all clients read from it individually, but it would require a round-trip through the filesystem, and it would introduce more failure cases).

+All authenticated users can start jobs - each job will have an associated owner - and they can only stop, get the status and read the output of their own jobs.
+
+API
+---
+The gRPC API is composed of a single `JobControl` service with four methods (`Start`, `Stop`, `GetInfo` and `StreamOutput`), detailed in [proto/jobcontrol.proto](proto/jobcontrol.proto). For simplicity, the API doesn't allow every cgroup parameter to be changed - for instance, the IO controller only allows `io.weight`.
+
+Design approach
+---------------
+A "job" consists of a program, with (optionally) some arguments, launched - if possible - in its own cgroup, with optional resource limits as decided by the client; we'll spawn the program with `/dev/null` as standard input, and a single pipe as standard output and error. Hopefully we can rely on `tokio::process::Command` to spawn the child (it's a wrapper around `std::process::Command`) and to allow us to asynchronously wait for it but as it's not cgroup-aware (and also somehow doesn't support the concept of spawning a pipe and passing it as both stdout and stderr, which is something that even **Python** can do) we'll have to run some fixups in a `pre_exec` closure, including adding the newly-created process to a newly-created cgroup, if we can. If that doesn't end up working out, we'll just write some abstraction that uses a pidfd for asynchronous waiting instead (and maybe use `clone3` to spawn the process directly in the correct cgroup, although that *does* require a pretty recent kernel version).
+
+We limit ourselves to handling cgroups v2 - a cgroups v1 implementation wouldn't be dramatically different, just more involved - and we expect to have an empty cgroup with available `cpu`, `memory` and `io` controllers, we expect to be able to create a subordinate cgroup inside of it (`job-<n>` where `n` is the job id), and we expect to be able to move our newly-created child process into such sub cgroup. This can be achieved even when running as user, for instance, by launching `challenged` in a systemd unit (or with `systemd-run`), enabling cgroup delegation - this will result in our process being the only process in a newly-created cgroup that we own; we'll then move ourselves into a sub-cgroup (maybe `control` or `worker`) and we'll enable subtree control on the root of our cgroup tree. This seems to be the sanest way of using cgroups for this sort of job control while running under systemd. If we are in condition to use cgroups, we'll create one for each job, right before spawning the child process, and we'll set the specified resource limits (if any); we will then move the newly created process into the cgroup before the execve.

+    config.alpn_protocols.push(b"h2".to_vec());
+
+    config
+}
+
+/// Returns a [`rustls::ClientConfig`] for use with Tonic, authenticating the
+/// server certificate against the root in `client_root`. Matching
+/// [`server_config`], only TLSv1.3 is enabled.
+///
+/// The certificate must be in DER format. Panics if the provided data is
+/// invalid.
+pub fn client_config<Der: Into<Vec<u8>>>(server_root: Der) -> rustls::ClientConfig {
+    let mut tls_config = rustls::ClientConfig::with_ciphersuites(&[
+        &rustls::ciphersuite::TLS13_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256,
+        &rustls::ciphersuite::TLS13_AES_256_GCM_SHA384,
+        &rustls::ciphersuite::TLS13_AES_128_GCM_SHA256,
+    ]);
+    tls_config.versions = vec![rustls::ProtocolVersion::TLSv1_3];
+
+    tls_config
+        .root_store
+        .add(&rustls::Certificate(server_root.into()))
+        .expect("bad root certificate");
+
+    tls_config.alpn_protocols.push(b"h2".to_vec());
+
+    tls_config
+}
+
+/// Intercepts a [`tonic::Request`] to either extract an [`Identity`] from the
+/// client's TLS certificate (inserting it in the `Request`'s extensions), or
+/// refuse the connection if no valid identity could be extracted.
+pub fn intercept_identity(
+    mut request: tonic::Request<()>,
+) -> Result<tonic::Request<()>, tonic::Status> {
+    // this should never happen, the transport layer should be taking care of
+    // ensuring that a valid client certificate was provided
+    let cert = request
+        .peer_certs()
+        .ok_or_else(|| tonic::Status::unauthenticated("no certificates found"))?;
+
+    // we're only interested in the end-entity certificate, which is the first one
+    let cert = cert
+        .iter()
+        .next()
+        .ok_or_else(|| tonic::Status::unauthenticated("no certificates found"))?;
+
+    let (rem, cert) = x509_parser::parse_x509_certificate(cert.as_ref()).map_err(|err| {
+        tonic::Status::internal(format!("failure to parse validated certificate: {}", err))
+    })?;
+    if !rem.is_empty() {
+        return Err(tonic::Status::internal(
+            "leftover data while parsing client certificate",
+        ));
+    }
+
+    request
+        .extensions_mut()
+        .insert(get_identity_from_cert(cert)?);
+
+    Ok(request)
+}
+
+/// Attempts to extract the username from a certificate. In case of failure,
+/// returns an [`io::Error`] with kind [`io::ErrorKind::InvalidData`].
+///
+/// Failure can happen (even from a valid certificate!) because we are very
+/// conservative in what sort of identity we accept from a certificate: we want
+/// an ascii-alphanumeric string from a unique Common Name in the certificate,
+/// and it's perfectly legal to have no CN or multiple CNs in a certificate, and
+/// it's perfectly legal to have an arbitrary unicode string there.
comment.body: Requiring that the identity is unique per-certificate is a matter of sanity, the restriction on the contents are mostly just a matter of style - if you allow arbitrary unicode you also have to address potential issues with canonicalization or lack thereof, I suppose.

pull_request.title: TLS support with authentication and a CLI tool
pull_request.body:
This adds encryption to both the server and a newly introduced CLI client. Encryption is mandatory, as it is used as the source of authentication.

Setting up the environment now requires launching the `generate.sh` script in `certs/`, so a README was also added to detail that.

pull_request.title: cgroup support and resource limits
pull_request.body:
This adds cgroup support to the service (when available) for job management and resource limits, and options to the CLI tool to request said limits.

The README describes how to get it to work as a regular user on systemd-based distros.

pull_request.title: Basic functionality
pull_request.body:
This includes the basic library functionality (not cgroup-aware) and the gRPC API (without encryption).

The library has tests (runnable with `cargo test`) whereas I've only tested the rpc side manually, as I'm waiting to implement some client layer first.
